title: Line Integrals
description: Line integrals (OpenStax 6.2, a 40 minute class): unroll a curve into the sheet under it to see the scalar line integral as a limit of sums, watch work build up as a point moves through a field, reverse the orientation and see the sign flip, split a rectangle into pieces, then compare flux and circulation on the same curve, with many verified examples.

steps.label: Scalar Line Integrals
steps.subtitle: Definition
steps.bodyHtml:
Definition: scalar line integral

Let \(f\) be a function with a domain that includes the smooth curve \(C\) parameterized by \(\vec r(t)=\langle x(t),y(t),z(t)\rangle\), \(a\le t\le b\). The scalar line integral of \(f\) along \(C\) is

$$\int_C f(x,y,z)\,ds=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(P_i^*)\,\Delta s_i$$

if this limit exists, where \(\Delta s_i\) is the length of the \(i\)th piece of \(C\) and \(P_i^*\) is a point in it.

Example 6.14. \(\int_C 2\,ds\), where \(C\) is the upper half of the unit circle.\(2\pi\)

steps.label: Evaluating a Scalar Line Integral
steps.subtitle: Theorems 6.3 and 6.4
steps.bodyHtml:
Theorem 6.4: Scalar Line Integral Calculation
$$\int_C f(x,y,z)\,ds=\int_a^b f(\vec r(t))\sqrt{(x'(t))^2+(y'(t))^2+(z'(t))^2}\,dt,\qquad ds=\|\vec r^{\prime}(t)\|\,dt.$$
Checkpoint 6.13. \(\int_C(x+y)\,ds\), \(x=t\), \(y=t\), \(0\le t\le1\).\(\sqrt2\)
Example 6.15. \(\int_C(x^2+y^2+z)\,ds\), \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t,t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\).\(\int_0^{2\pi}(1+t)\sqrt2\,dt=2\sqrt2\,\pi+2\sqrt2\,\pi^2\)
Example 6.16. The same integral with \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos2t,\sin2t,2t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le\pi\).\(2\sqrt2\int_0^\pi(1+2t)\,dt=2\sqrt2(\pi+\pi^2)\), the same value
Checkpoint 6.15. \(\int_C(x^2+yz)\,ds\), \(\vec r(t)=\langle2t,5t,-t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le10\).\(-\dfrac{1000\sqrt{30}}{3}\)

steps.label: Arc Length and Mass of a Wire
steps.subtitle: Examples 6.17, 6.22
steps.bodyHtml:
Arc length

\(\displaystyle\int_C 1\,ds=\text{length}(C)\)

Mass of a wire with linear density \(\rho(x,y,z)\)

\(\displaystyle\text{mass}=\int_C\rho(x,y,z)\,ds\)

Example 6.17. Length of the wire \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t,\tfrac23t^{3/2}\rangle\), \(0\le t\le4\pi\).\(\int_0^{4\pi}\sqrt{1+t}\,dt=\dfrac23\big((1+4\pi)^{3/2}-1\big)\)
Checkpoint 6.16. Length of \(\vec r(t)=\langle3t+1,\,4-2t,\,5+2t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le4\).\(4\sqrt{17}\)
Example 6.22. Mass of the spring \(\langle t,2\cos t,2\sin t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le\tfrac\pi2\), with \(\rho=e^x+yz\) kg/m.\(\sqrt5\,(e^{\pi/2}+1)\) kg
Exercise 54. Mass of a circle of radius \(2\) centered at \((3,4)\) with \(\rho(x,y)=y^2\).\(72\pi\)

steps.label: Vector Line Integrals
steps.subtitle: Orientation and work
steps.bodyHtml:
Orientation

A specified direction along \(C\) is an orientation; \(C\) is then an oriented curve. \(-C\) is the same curve with the opposite orientation. A closed curve has a parameterization with \(\vec r(a)=\vec r(b)\), traversed exactly once.

Definition: vector line integral
$$\int_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf T\,ds=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^n\vec F(P_i^*)\cdot\mathbf T(P_i^*)\,\Delta s_i$$

The work done by \(\vec F\) moving a particle in the positive direction along \(C\) is \(W=\int_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf T\,ds\).

steps.label: Evaluating a Vector Line Integral
steps.subtitle: Equation 6.9
steps.bodyHtml:
Equation 6.9
$$\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf T\,ds=\int_a^b\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\vec r^{\prime}(t)\,dt,\qquad \int_{-C}\vec F\cdot d\vec r=-\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r.$$
Example 6.18. \(\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\), \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le\pi\), \(\vec F=\langle-y,x\rangle\).\(\int_0^\pi1\,dt=\pi\)
Example 6.19. The same field with \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos(t+\pi),\sin t\rangle\), \(0\le t\le\pi\).\(-\pi\)
Checkpoint 6.17. \(\vec F=x\,\mathbf i+y\,\mathbf j\), \(C:\langle t,t^2\rangle\), \(0\le t\le2\). Which is greater, \(\int_C\) or \(\int_{-C}\)?\(\int_C=10\), \(\int_{-C}=-10\)

steps.label: The Form P dx + Q dy + R dz
steps.subtitle: Equation 6.10
steps.bodyHtml:
Equation 6.10
$$\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz=\int\Big(P\frac{dx}{dt}+Q\frac{dy}{dt}+R\frac{dz}{dt}\Big)dt$$
Example 6.20. \(\int_C z\,dx+x\,dy+y\,dz\), \(\vec r(t)=\langle t^2,\sqrt t,t\rangle\), \(1\le t\le4\).\(\dfrac{793}{15}\)
Checkpoint 6.18. \(\int_C4x\,dx+z\,dy+4y^2\,dz\), \(\vec r(t)=\langle4\cos2t,2\sin2t,3\rangle\), \(0\le t\le\tfrac\pi4\).\(-26\)

steps.label: Piecewise Smooth Curves
steps.subtitle: Theorem 6.5
steps.bodyHtml:
Piecewise smooth curve

\(C=C_1+C_2+\cdots+C_n\), smooth curves where the endpoint of \(C_i\) is the starting point of \(C_{i+1}\).

Theorem 6.5: Properties of Vector Line Integrals

i. \(\int_C(\vec F+\vec G)\cdot d\vec r=\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r+\int_C\vec G\cdot d\vec r\)   ii. \(\int_C k\vec F\cdot d\vec r=k\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\)   iii. \(\int_{-C}\vec F\cdot d\vec r=-\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\)

iv. \(\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_{C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r+\cdots+\int_{C_n}\vec F\cdot d\vec r\)

Example 6.21. \(\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\), \(C\) the rectangle with vertices \((0,0),(2,0),(2,1),(0,1)\) counterclockwise, \(\vec F=\langle x-2y,\,y-x\rangle\).\(2-\tfrac32+2-\tfrac12=2\)
Checkpoint 6.19. \(\vec F=\langle y^2,\,2xy+1\rangle\), \(C\) the triangle \((0,0),(4,0),(0,5)\) counterclockwise.\(0+5-5=0\)

steps.label: Work Done by a Force
steps.subtitle: Example 6.23
steps.bodyHtml:
Work

An object moves along \(C\) in force field \(\vec F\): \(\;W=\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\).

Example 6.23. Work done by \(\vec F=\langle yz,xy,xz\rangle\) along \(\vec r(t)=\langle t^2,t,t^4\rangle\), \(0\le t\le1\).\(\dfrac{131}{140}\)
Exercise 65. \(\vec F=-x\,\mathbf i-2y\,\mathbf j\) along \(y=x^3\) from \((0,0)\) to \((2,8)\).\(-66\)
Exercise 98. \(\vec F=(x+2y)\,\mathbf i+(-x+y^2)\,\mathbf j\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). David: along the \(x\)-axis, then up \(x=1\). Sandra: along \(y=x\). Whose is larger?David \(-\tfrac16\), Sandra \(\tfrac43\). Sandra's is larger by \(\tfrac32\)

steps.label: Flux Across a Curve
steps.subtitle: Definition, Theorem 6.6
steps.bodyHtml:
Definition: flux

For \(\vec r(t)=\langle x(t),y(t)\rangle\), let \(\mathbf n(t)=\langle y'(t),-x'(t)\rangle\) (normal, pointing right of the direction of travel) and \(\mathbf N=\mathbf n/\|\mathbf n\|\). The flux of \(\vec F\) across \(C\) is \(\int_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf N\,ds\).

Theorem 6.6: Calculating Flux across a Curve
$$\int_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf N\,ds=\int_a^b\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\mathbf n(t)\,dt$$
Example 6.24. Flux of \(\vec F=\langle2x,2y\rangle\) across the unit circle, counterclockwise.\(4\pi\)
Checkpoint 6.21. Flux of \(\vec F=\langle x+y,2y\rangle\) across the segment from \((0,0)\) to \((2,3)\), left to right.\(\tfrac32\)
Exercise 89. \(\vec F=5\,\mathbf j\), \(C:\ y=0\), \(0\le x\le4\).\(-20\)

steps.label: Circulation
steps.subtitle: Examples 6.25, 6.26
steps.bodyHtml:
Circulation

The line integral of \(\vec F\) along an oriented closed curve is the circulation of \(\vec F\) along \(C\), written \(\oint_C\vec F\cdot\mathbf T\,ds\).

Example 6.25. Circulation of \(\vec F=\langle-y,x\rangle\) along the unit circle, counterclockwise (and clockwise).\(2\pi\) (and \(-2\pi\))
Example 6.26. Work done by \(\vec F=\langle-2,y\rangle\) around the circle of radius \(2\), counterclockwise.\(0\)
Checkpoint 6.22. Circulation of \(\Big\langle-\dfrac y{x^2+y^2},\dfrac x{x^2+y^2}\Big\rangle\) along the unit circle, counterclockwise.\(2\pi\)
